cues.en: Welcome to Class 6: electronic materials, energy bands and doping.
In Class 2 we said that silicon sits between conductors and insulators, and that doping can move it. Today we see why, and by how much.
We will meet electrons and holes, and see how one atom in five million changes the resistivity of silicon about half a million times.
If you are studying on your own, the narration takes about eleven minutes. Stop at the activity and at each check, then do Lab 6.
Here is the plan for today.
A five minute activity reviews earlier classes.
Part one is about bands: how energy levels merge into bands in a solid, and how they separate conductors, semiconductors and insulators. It ends with Check 1.
Part two is about doping: donors and acceptors, the balance between electrons and holes, resistivity, charge neutrality, and purity. It ends with Check 2.
Then you do Lab 6 for thirty minutes, and finish with the Exit Ticket.
Activity 1. Answer four questions without notes, then compare with a partner.
Give the valence electrons of boron, silicon and phosphorus. Estimate the silicon atoms in one cubic centimeter.
Find the hydroxide concentration when the hydrogen ion concentration is ten to the minus three. And recall the resistivity of pure silicon.
Pause the narration now, write your answers, and then press Show answers.
By the end of today you can use band diagrams to tell conductors, semiconductors and insulators apart.
You can describe electrons and holes as the two carriers in silicon.
You can explain why phosphorus is a donor and boron an acceptor, and name the majority carrier in each.
You can use the product rule for electrons and holes to find the minority carrier concentration.
And you can calculate the resistivity of doped silicon, and explain why n type silicon has no net charge.
Today explains silicon's place in the resistivity chart of Class 2.
From Class 3 we know there are about five times ten to the twenty two silicon atoms per cubic centimeter, so we can compare carriers and dopants with that number.
And from Class 5, the product of hydrogen and hydroxide concentrations is fixed. A product rule of the same kind links electrons and holes.
New symbols: E g is the band gap in electron volts. n and p are the concentrations of free electrons and holes, per cubic centimeter. n i is their value in pure silicon.
And mu is mobility, how easily a carrier moves.
When atoms join into a solid, their energy levels merge into bands. Bands are ranges of energy that electrons may have, not layers inside the material.
To carry current, an electron needs an empty state close in energy.
In a metal such as copper, one band is only partly filled, so empty states sit right above the filled ones, and electrons move easily.
In silicon, a filled valence band and an empty conduction band are separated by a gap of one point one two electron volts. At room temperature, a few electrons are lifted across it.
In silicon dioxide, the gap is about nine electron volts, too large for electrons to cross.
But the gap alone does not give the conductivity. That also needs how many carriers there are, and how easily they move.
When an electron leaves a silicon bond, it becomes free to move. That is a conduction electron, with charge minus e.
The bond it left is short one electron. We call that a hole.
A neighboring bond electron can hop into the hole, so the hole moves the other way. It behaves like a mobile positive charge.
Think of a row of seats with one empty seat. As each person moves toward it, the empty seat moves the other way along the row.
So silicon has two carriers: electrons and holes. Holes move about three times more slowly than electrons.
How many carriers does pure silicon have? At room temperature, n and p are both about one point four five times ten to the ten per cubic centimeter.
Compared with five times ten to the twenty two atoms, that is only about three atoms in ten to the thirteen giving up an electron.
Multiply the carriers by the elementary charge and their mobilities to get the conductivity.
The resistivity is about two point three five times ten to the five ohm centimeters, which is the value we used in Class 2.
This intrinsic carrier concentration rises steeply with temperature. A device whose current changed that much with temperature would be useless, so doping fixes the carrier count on purpose.
Check 1. Answer these four questions on your own, in about five minutes.
Match three band diagrams to conductor, semiconductor and insulator. Say whether the gap alone gives the conductivity. Describe a hole. And give n and p in pure silicon.
Pause now, write your answers, and then press Show answers.
Part 2 is about doping. Replace one silicon atom with phosphorus.
Phosphorus has five valence electrons. Four form bonds with silicon neighbors, and the fifth is easily freed.
Phosphorus is a donor, and the silicon becomes n type, with electrons as the majority carriers. A fixed positive phosphorus ion stays behind.
Now replace a silicon atom with boron. Boron has only three valence electrons for four bonds, so it takes one from a neighbor and creates a hole.
Boron is an acceptor, and the silicon becomes p type, with holes as the majority carriers.
Arsenic is also a donor, and aluminum an acceptor.
How many carriers does doping give? Each donor gives one electron, so n is about equal to the donor concentration.
Then the holes follow from the product rule: n times p equals n i squared, about two times ten to the twenty.
With ten to the sixteen donors, there are only about two times ten to the four holes.
Move the slider. As the majority carriers rise, the minority carriers fall, and their product stays the same, just like hydrogen and hydroxide ions in water.
With ten to the sixteen phosphorus atoms per cubic centimeter, the resistivity falls to about zero point four six ohm centimeters, about half a million times lower than pure silicon.
This model keeps the mobility constant. At very high doping, real mobility falls, so real resistivity is a little higher.
Here is a common mistake: n type silicon has extra electrons, so it carries a negative charge.
Each phosphorus atom brings one extra electron, but also one extra proton in its nucleus. When the electron is freed, a fixed positive ion stays behind.
So in a model with five donors, the ions carry plus five and the free electrons minus five. The total is zero. The name n type describes the majority carrier, not the charge.
Charge appears only where n type and p type regions meet, and that is how diodes and transistors work.
How little dopant is needed? Ten to the sixteen phosphorus atoms among five times ten to the twenty two silicon atoms is two times ten to the minus seven:
one phosphorus atom per about five million silicon atoms.
That tiny amount cut the resistivity half a million times. Doping is added on purpose, in measured amounts and places.
If so little phosphorus changes silicon this much, unwanted atoms do too. Metals such as copper, iron and sodium can ruin devices at parts per billion.
That is why copper wiring is sealed off from silicon, and why fabs rinse wafers in ultrapure water.
Check 2. Answer these four questions on your own, in about five minutes.
Classify phosphorus and boron. Find n and p for ten to the sixteen donors. Find the total charge of a doped model. And explain why copper must be kept away from silicon.
Pause now, write your answers, and then press Show answers.
Today closes the materials block and opens the electrochemistry block.
Class 7 moves electrons between species, not just within a solid. Class 8 sends electrons through a wire and ions through an electrolyte.
Class 11 looks at charge that builds up where two materials meet. And in the second half of the course, band gaps return in semiconductors that split water with light.
Now it is time for Lab 6. Scan the code or open the lab page.
You will predict whether phosphorus is a donor, classify phosphorus and boron, and check that doped silicon is neutral.
Then you find the dopant fraction and the minority carriers, change the doping to find the resistivity, and match band diagrams to materials.
The lab takes about thirty minutes. Pause the narration now and work through it.
Here is a summary of today.
Conductors have no gap, semiconductors a small gap, and insulators a large gap, but the gap alone is not the conductivity.
Silicon has two carriers, electrons and holes.
Phosphorus donates electrons and makes n type silicon. Boron accepts electrons and makes p type silicon, with holes as the majority.
The product of electrons and holes stays n i squared, so more majority carriers mean fewer minority carriers.
And doped silicon stays neutral, while tiny amounts of atoms, wanted or not, change it a great deal.
